usage: 우리 (our) is the default possessive Koreans use even for 'my' family
literally 'family is many' — use 많다, not 크다, for member count
two nouns stacked directly, no 의 needed

nuance: 가족 is the Sino-Korean word 家族 ('house' 家 + 'clan/group' 族), so it names the whole family unit as a collective, never a single relative — for one member you must say 가족 한 명 or name the relationship (형, 누나). The near-synonym 식구 also means family but literally means 食口 'mouths to feed', stressing the people who live and eat under one roof, so 식구 feels warmer and more domestic ('우리 식구 다섯이에요') while 가족 is the neutral standard term that also covers relatives living apart. Register is neutral and safe in any setting. The big English-speaker trap is two-fold: 'big/small family' is 가족이 많다/적다 (many/few), never 가족이 크다 (that sounds like physically large bodies); and Koreans say 우리 가족 ('our family') where English forces 'my family', so the 우리 is idiomatic, not a mistake.

usage: 우리 + the built-in honorific 님 = the polite default
use 계시다, the honorific of 있다, to match 님
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테, required by 님
댁 is the honorific of 집 (house)
examples: 살다 (to live/reside) drops its ㄹ before some endings but keeps it in 살아요
I call my parents every day.
드리다 is the humble form of 주다/하다 — you 'give' the call up to elders
My parents are in Busan right now.
계세요 (honorific 있어요) is obligatory because the subject is 부모님
nuance: 부모님 is Sino-Korean 父母 ('father' 父 + 'mother' 母) plus the honorific suffix 님, so the respect is baked into the word itself and it is the everyday polite default — there is no need to add anything to make it courteous. The bare root 부모 exists but is abstract and institutional ('부모의 역할' the role of parents, '부모 교육' parenting education); aimed at a real person it sounds cold, so for your own or anyone's parents you say 부모님. Because 님 marks the referent as worthy of respect, every verb around it must climb to its honorific tier: 있다→계시다, 주다→드리다, 집→댁, 에게→께, and the topic/subject can even take 께서. The classic English-speaker pitfall is pairing 부모님 with plain verbs ('부모님이 있어요', '부모님한테 줬어요'); grammatically the words exist, but to a Korean ear it clashes like saying 'Her Majesty ate fast' — you must use 계세요 and 드렸어요/께.

usage: 우리 'our' is the natural possessive even for one's own mother
엄마 takes 가 as the thing-liked with 좋다
돕다 is ㅂ-irregular: 돕 + 아요 → 도와요
한테 is the casual dative that suits this intimate word
examples: 잘하다 = 잘 (well) + 하다, written as one word
좋아하다 (verb, takes 를) acts on 엄마, unlike adjective 좋다 (takes 가)

nuance: 엄마 is the warm, intimate nursery word for 'mother', the everyday home register you use speaking to her directly or about her among family and friends — emotionally it is exactly English 'mom/mommy'. Its formal counterpart is 어머니, the respectful word for polite or public settings (introducing her, speaking to in-laws, addressing a friend's mother as 어머니); think of the pair as a sliding scale, 엄마 (intimate) → 어머니 (formal/respectful). Unlike 부모님, 엄마 has no honorific 님 built in, so it stays in the casual zone, though you still naturally use it with polite -요 endings ('엄마가 와요'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 엄마 as a neutral all-purpose 'mother': calling a stranger's mother 엄마, or saying 엄마 to your boss when reporting on a parent, feels childish or over-familiar — switch up to 어머니 the moment the situation turns formal, just as English shifts from 'my mom' to 'my mother'.

usage: 우리 'our' is the idiomatic possessive for one's own father

한테 is the casual, affectionate dative

다니다 means to attend/commute to regularly; pairs with 에

닮다 uses 를 + past 았어요; the resemblance is stated as completed

nuance: 아빠 is the affectionate home word for 'father', the casual nursery register matching English 'dad/daddy', used to him directly and about him in relaxed company. Its formal partner is 아버지, the respectful term for public or polite situations — introductions, talking to elders, a friend's father — so the pair runs 아빠 (intimate) → 아버지 (formal), exactly mirroring 엄마 → 어머니. Like 엄마, it carries no honorific 님, so it lives in the casual zone but still combines with polite -요 endings. A frequent and very Korean collocation is 닮다 'to resemble' — 아빠를 닮다 'take after dad' — and note it takes the object particle 를, where English-speakers often wrongly reach for 'with' (와/하고). usage: said only by a male; the word itself signals the speaker is male
있다 = 'have/exist'; 형 takes 가→이 after a consonant
한테 is the casual dative used among close family
친 (親, 'blood/real') distinguishes him from a 사촌 or 의형
examples: 명 counts people; one says 한 명, never 일 명
I play games with my older brother.
하고 (casual 'with') + 같이 is the everyday combo for 'together with'

보다 = 'than'; literally 'than me, height is big' = taller
nuance: 형 (Sino-Korean 兄 'elder brother') is the word a MALE uses for an older brother, and crucially it is also a warm address term a younger man uses for any slightly-older male he is close to — an older friend, schoolmate, or colleague — so '민수 형' can mean 'Minsu, my big-brother-figure', not a blood relative. The matched set is gendered by speaker: a female says 오빠 for the same older-brother relationship, while 누나/언니 cover older sisters — so the single word leaks the speaker's gender, something English's flat 'older brother' never does. Register is casual-but-respectful: 형 is itself an honorific address (you call him 형, never his bare name), and you speak up to him. The dominant English-speaker pitfall is gender: a woman must never call her older brother 형 — that is 오빠 — and second, don't assume 형 always means kin; in daily life it is most often the affectionate title for an older male friend.

nuance: 남편 (Sino-Korean 男便, lit. 'male side') is the standard, neutral word for 'husband', used for your own husband and, in plain speech, anyone's. To speak respectfully about ANOTHER person's husband you add the honorific counter 분 → 남편분 ('your husband'), much as 부모→부모님 climbs in politeness. Distinguish it sharply from 신랑 'groom/hubby', which literally means the bridegroom but is also used affectionately or by newlyweds for a husband, and from the blunt third-person 그 남자 — 남편 is the safe everyday choice. The decisive English-speaker pitfall is the boyfriend/husband line: 남편 means a legally married spouse only, so a girlfriend's partner is 남자친구, NOT 남편 — English casually says 'my man/my partner', but in Korean 남편 firmly implies marriage. Also, when honoring someone else's spouse, don't leave it as bare 남편; use 남편분 to stay polite.

nuance: 아내 is the standard, slightly warm native word for one's own 'wife', the safe default in most speech. Its near-synonyms divide cleanly: 와이프 (from English 'wife') is very common in casual male conversation but too informal for formal writing; 부인 (夫人) is the POLITE word for ANOTHER man's wife ('사장님 부인') and sounds odd for your own; and 집사람/안사람 are older, humble self-references ('the person of the house') now fading and faintly old-fashioned. So the map is: 아내/와이프 = my wife (neutral/casual), 부인 = your wife (polite). The key English-speaker pitfall is the girlfriend/wife line: 아내 means a married spouse, so an unmarried partner is 여자친구, not 아내 — English 'my partner' blurs this, Korean does not. A second trap is calling your own wife 부인; reserve 부인 for politely referring to someone else's wife.

nuance: 아이 means 'child' in the broad sense — your own kid or any young person — and is routinely contracted to 애 in casual speech ('우리 애가…'), which is natural but a touch more colloquial. Pin down the age band against its neighbors: 아기 (or 애기) is a baby/infant who can't yet walk or talk; 아이/애 is a child roughly from toddler through pre-teen; 어린이 is the more formal, respectful 'child' used on signs and in institutions (어린이날 Children's Day, 어린이 보호구역 school zone); and 자녀 is the formal Sino-Korean word for one's offspring used on forms ('자녀가 몇 명이세요?'). So 아이 sits in the middle, neutral-casual. The main English-speaker pitfall is mixing 아이 with 아기: English 'kid/child/baby' overlap loosely, but calling a 10-year-old 아기 sounds like babying them, and calling a newborn 아이 understates how tiny they are — match the word to the age.
